body:
Meaning of planetary winds

Planetary winds are large-scale prevailing winds that develop between the major pressure belts of the Earth. They arise from atmospheric pressure differences, while Earth's rotation modifies their direction.

They are also called permanent winds or prevailing winds because their general directions persist throughout the year. Their actual speed, position and direction can nevertheless vary with season and regional atmospheric conditions.

There are 3 principal planetary wind systems: trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.

Trade winds

Trade winds are tropical easterly winds that blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low-pressure belt.

Northeast trade winds

In the Northern Hemisphere, air moving from the subtropical high near 30° N towards the Equator is deflected to its right. The resulting prevailing wind comes from the northeast and moves towards the southwest.

Southeast trade winds

In the Southern Hemisphere, air moving from the subtropical high near 30° S towards the Equator is deflected to its left. The resulting prevailing wind comes from the southeast and moves towards the northwest.

Both trade-wind systems therefore possess a westward component of motion and converge in the equatorial low-pressure region.

Trade winds are relatively regular over extensive tropical oceans. Historically, sailing ships used these dependable winds for westward voyages across the Atlantic and other tropical oceans. The name trade winds comes from the older meaning of trade as a regular course, referring to their steady direction.

Trade winds can acquire substantial moisture while travelling over warm oceans. When this moisture-bearing air rises through convergence or over elevated terrain, it may produce considerable rainfall.

Westerlies

Westerlies are the prevailing winds of the middle latitudes, approximately between 30° and 60° in both hemispheres. They blow from subtropical high-pressure belts towards subpolar low-pressure belts.

  • In the Northern Hemisphere, their prevailing direction is from southwest towards northeast.
  • In the Southern Hemisphere, their prevailing direction is from northwest towards southeast.

Unlike trade winds, westerlies possess an eastward component of motion. They are generally less regular in direction and speed because middle latitudes experience frequent atmospheric disturbances.

Why Southern Hemisphere westerlies are stronger

The Southern Hemisphere has much greater expanses of ocean in its middle latitudes and fewer continental obstacles. Westerly winds can therefore circulate more continuously and are generally stronger than their Northern Hemisphere counterparts.

Traditional maritime names for particularly strong southern winds include:

  • Roaring Forties: approximately 40° S to 50° S.
  • Furious Fifties: approximately 50° S to 60° S.
  • Screaming Sixties: strong winds in the vicinity of the 60° S latitudes, also called the Screeching Sixties.

These are traditional geographical and maritime expressions, not strictly defined atmospheric pressure or wind belts.

Polar easterlies

Polar easterlies blow from polar high-pressure regions towards subpolar low-pressure regions, approximately between 90° and 60° latitude in each hemisphere.

  • In the Northern Hemisphere, they generally blow from northeast towards southwest.
  • In the Southern Hemisphere, they generally blow from southeast towards northwest.

Polar easterlies originate in very cold regions and generally contain little moisture. Their convergence with the relatively warmer westerlies near the subpolar region contributes to ascending air along the polar front.

Comparison of planetary wind systems

WindApprox. latitudeNorthern Hemisphere originSouthern Hemisphere origin
Trade winds0°–30°NortheastSoutheast
Westerlies30°–60°SouthwestNorthwest
Polar easterlies60°–90°NortheastSoutheast

Trade winds and polar easterlies have similar prevailing compass directions within the same hemisphere. However, they originate from different high-pressure belts, occupy different latitudes and possess different temperature characteristics.

The subtropical high-pressure belt is the common source region of both trade winds and westerlies. Trade winds move equatorward, whereas westerlies move poleward from this belt.

Prelims focus

  • Trade winds: subtropical highs to equatorial low.
  • Westerlies: subtropical highs to subpolar lows.
  • Polar easterlies: polar highs to subpolar lows.
  • Trade winds and polar easterlies have a westward component; westerlies have an eastward component.
  • Roaring Forties and Furious Fifties are associated with strong Southern Hemisphere winds.
  • Trap: Northeast trade winds and northeast polar easterlies are distinct wind systems despite their similar directions.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 4: Air, Fig. 4.4, p. 25; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 10: Winds, pp. 70–71; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 9, Fig. 9.6, p. 80; NOAA National Ocean Service, What Are the Trade Winds? and What Are the Roaring Forties? Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

body:
Why the atmosphere circulates globally

Equatorial regions receive more solar energy than polar regions. This uneven distribution of heat creates temperature and pressure differences that drive large-scale atmospheric circulation.

Atmospheric circulation transports heat and moisture between different latitudes, helping redistribute the energy received by the Earth.

In the absence of Earth's rotation, a much simpler circulation might develop between the Equator and the poles. On the rotating Earth, the general circulation is conventionally explained through a simplified three-cell model.

Each hemisphere contains 3 major circulation cells in this model: the Hadley cell, the Ferrel cell and the Polar cell. Together, the 2 hemispheres contain 6 cells.

Hadley cell

The Hadley cell operates approximately between the Equator and 30° latitude in each hemisphere.

  1. Strong equatorial heating causes air to rise near the equatorial low-pressure belt.
  2. The rising air spreads towards the subtropics in the upper troposphere.
  3. Part of the air descends near 30° latitude, contributing to the subtropical high-pressure belt.
  4. Some surface air returns towards the Equator as trade winds, completing the circulation.

The Hadley cell therefore connects the humid, ascending equatorial region with the generally dry, descending subtropical region.

Ferrel cell

The Ferrel cell operates approximately between 30° and 60° latitude in each hemisphere.

In the simplified circulation model, surface air flows poleward from the subtropical high-pressure belt towards the subpolar low-pressure belt. Coriolis deflection produces the prevailing westerlies.

Air generally ascends near the subpolar region and returns equatorward at higher levels, with descent occurring in the subtropical region.

The Ferrel cell is a thermally indirect circulation cell: air rises in the cooler subpolar region and sinks in the warmer subtropics. Unlike the Hadley and Polar cells, its average circulation is strongly influenced by atmospheric disturbances and the movement of contrasting air masses in the middle latitudes.

Polar cell

The Polar cell operates approximately between 60° and 90° latitude in each hemisphere.

Intense cooling near the poles produces cold, dense air that descends and contributes to polar high pressure. Surface air moves equatorward as polar easterlies.

Near the subpolar region, this air meets the relatively warmer air associated with the westerlies. Ascent occurs near the subpolar low-pressure belt, and air returns towards the poles at higher levels.

Comparison of the 3 circulation cells

CellLatitudeSurface wind
Hadley cell0°–30°Trade winds
Ferrel cell30°–60°Westerlies
Polar cell60°–90°Polar easterlies

Shared boundaries of circulation cells

The boundaries between neighbouring cells help explain the location of the major pressure belts.

  • Near 0°, the 2 Hadley cells meet through ascending equatorial air.
  • Near 30° in each hemisphere, the Hadley and Ferrel cells share a region of descending air and relatively high pressure.
  • Near 60° in each hemisphere, the Ferrel and Polar cells meet near a region of convergence, ascent and relatively low pressure.
  • Near 90°, descending air maintains polar high-pressure conditions.

The three-cell model represents average atmospheric behaviour. Actual winds and vertical air movements are more variable and are modified by seasons, oceans, continents and regional weather systems.

Prelims focus

  • 3 major atmospheric circulation cells per hemisphere; 6 globally.
  • Hadley cell: 0°–30°, associated with trade winds.
  • Ferrel cell: 30°–60°, associated with westerlies.
  • Polar cell: 60°–90°, associated with polar easterlies.
  • Hadley and Ferrel cells share the descending subtropical region.
  • Ferrel and Polar cells share the ascending subpolar region.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 9: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems, General Circulation of the Atmosphere, pp. 79–80 and Fig. 9.6; UK Met Office, Global Circulation Patterns. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

title: General Atmospheric Circulation: Hadley, Ferrel and Polar Cells

body:
Meaning of the ITCZ

The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a broad, shifting zone of low-level wind convergence in tropical latitudes, associated with ascending air, extensive cloud formation and frequent precipitation.

In the conventional planetary wind system, northeast trade winds from the Northern Hemisphere and southeast trade winds from the Southern Hemisphere meet in the equatorial region. Their convergence is a characteristic feature of the ITCZ.

The ITCZ is closely associated with the equatorial low-pressure belt and forms the ascending tropical portion of the general atmospheric circulation.

Formation of the ITCZ

  1. Strong solar heating warms the tropical surface and the air above it.
  2. Warm air expands and rises, contributing to relatively low surface pressure.
  3. Trade winds transport air towards the low-pressure region.
  4. The converging air ascends, expands and cools.
  5. Where sufficient moisture is present, water vapour condenses, producing clouds and precipitation.

The ITCZ is particularly prominent over warm tropical oceans, where converging winds often supply substantial moisture.

Weather associated with the ITCZ

The combination of moisture, convergence and strong upward air movement frequently produces tall clouds, heavy convectional rainfall and thunderstorms.

Although trade winds converge towards this region, surface winds within the convergence zone may be weak or irregular. A weak horizontal surface wind does not imply that the atmosphere is inactive. Strong vertical air movement can occur at the same time.

The arrival and departure of the ITCZ contribute to the alternating wet and dry seasons experienced by many tropical regions.

Doldrums and horse latitudes

Both the equatorial low-pressure region and the subtropical high-pressure regions have historically been associated with weak or variable surface winds that could delay sailing ships. However, their atmospheric processes and typical weather conditions differ considerably.

CharacteristicDoldrumsHorse latitudes
LocationNear EquatorNear 30° N and S
PressureLowHigh
Surface movementConvergenceDivergence
Vertical movementAscending airDescending air
Typical conditionsHumid and rainyGenerally dry and clear

The doldrums describe the traditionally calm or variable wind conditions associated with the equatorial low-pressure region. The ITCZ describes the physical atmospheric zone of tropical convergence and ascent. The terms are closely related but emphasise different characteristics.

Horse latitudes, in contrast, are associated with subtropical subsidence and high pressure. They are also the source regions of trade winds and westerlies.

Is the ITCZ permanently located at the Equator?

No. The geographical Equator is fixed at 0° latitude, whereas the ITCZ is an atmospheric feature whose location changes with the seasonal distribution of heating, ocean temperatures and the distribution of land and water.

The region of highest average temperature is sometimes described as the thermal equator. Its position need not coincide exactly with the geographical Equator. The ITCZ broadly responds to the changing distribution of tropical heating but is not identical to the thermal equator.

Prelims focus

  • ITCZ is a tropical convergence and low-pressure zone.
  • It is conventionally associated with the meeting of northeast and southeast trade winds.
  • Ascending moist air frequently produces clouds, thunderstorms and rainfall.
  • Doldrums are associated with equatorial low pressure; horse latitudes with subtropical high pressure.
  • The ITCZ migrates seasonally.
  • Trap: Weak horizontal winds in the doldrums do not imply an absence of vertical air movement.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 9, General Circulation of the Atmosphere, p. 80; NASA Earth Observatory, The Intertropical Convergence Zone; NOAA National Ocean Service, What Are the Doldrums? and What Are the Horse Latitudes?; UK Met Office, Intertropical Convergence Zone. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Trade winds converge in the tropical low-pressure zone; heated moist air rises, cools and brings rain despite weak surface winds.
pictures.caption: Trade-wind convergence and convectional rainfall in the ITCZ.

title: Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and Equatorial Weather

body:
Why pressure belts change their position

The Earth revolves around the Sun with its rotational axis tilted by approximately 23.5° from the perpendicular to its orbital plane. This axial tilt causes the latitude receiving the Sun's vertical rays to change throughout the year.

Because atmospheric heating varies seasonally, the zones of relatively high and low pressure also change their position.

In the conventional global pattern, pressure belts and their associated wind systems generally migrate towards the hemisphere experiencing summer and retreat towards the opposite hemisphere during winter.

Northward and southward migration

Northern Hemisphere summer

Around the June solstice, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun. The Sun's vertical rays reach the Tropic of Cancer at approximately 23.5° N.

In response to increased heating north of the Equator, the tropical convergence zone and associated circulation generally shift northward. The northern displacement of the ITCZ becomes particularly pronounced over strongly heated continental regions during the summer months.

Southern Hemisphere summer

Around the December solstice, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun. The Sun's vertical rays reach the Tropic of Capricorn at approximately 23.5° S.

The ITCZ and associated tropical circulation generally shift southward in response to seasonal heating. This coincides with winter in the Northern Hemisphere.

Equinoxes

Around the March and September equinoxes, the Sun's vertical rays fall on the geographical Equator. The tropical heating pattern transitions between its northern and southern seasonal positions.

However, the actual ITCZ need not lie exactly along the Equator on these dates. Atmospheric and oceanic conditions influence its location.

Continental and oceanic differences

Land surfaces generally heat and cool more rapidly than oceans. Oceans absorb, store and redistribute considerable amounts of heat, reducing the extent of seasonal surface temperature changes.

Consequently, the seasonal displacement of the ITCZ is often more pronounced over large tropical continents than over oceans.

For example, the ITCZ moves substantially northward over parts of Africa and South Asia during Northern Hemisphere summer. During Southern Hemisphere summer, it tends to migrate southward over parts of South America, southern tropical Africa and northern Australia.

Over oceanic regions, the displacement is often smaller. In some ocean basins, the ITCZ may remain predominantly north of the geographical Equator even when its position shifts southward seasonally.

Seasonal movement is not uniform

The ITCZ does not follow the Sun's vertical rays exactly. Its position is affected by differences in land and ocean heating, sea-surface temperatures and atmospheric circulation. The extent and timing of its migration vary geographically.

Effect on tropical rainfall

As the ITCZ moves into a tropical region, the likelihood of convergence, ascending moist air and rainfall generally increases. When it moves away, the region may experience comparatively drier conditions.

This migration helps produce the contrasting wet and dry seasons of many tropical savanna regions.

Places close to the Equator may experience 2 rainfall maxima during the year if the ITCZ passes over them during its northward and southward movements. Places farther from the Equator commonly experience one principal rainy season. These patterns are general tendencies rather than universal rules.

Seasonal movement and planetary winds

Because trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies are connected to the major pressure belts, shifts in pressure distribution also change the regions in which these winds prevail.

The most pronounced regional changes can produce seasonal reversals of winds, as observed in the monsoon circulation of South Asia.

Prelims focus

  • Earth's axial tilt is approximately 23.5° from the perpendicular to its orbital plane.
  • June solstice: vertical solar rays near 23.5° N.
  • December solstice: vertical solar rays near 23.5° S.
  • The ITCZ generally migrates northward during Northern Hemisphere summer and southward during Southern Hemisphere summer.
  • Its seasonal displacement is often greater over continents than oceans.
  • Trap: The ITCZ does not necessarily coincide with the latitude receiving vertical solar rays.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 3: Motions of the Earth, pp. 18–20; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 9, pp. 77–80, Figs. 9.2 and 9.3; UK Met Office, Intertropical Convergence Zone; NASA Earth Observatory, The Intertropical Convergence Zone. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]
